Warning: ramblings on English usage follow. Please don't downvoat.

Former means that the person stopped being whatever it is: it's usually used with various jobs (e.g., former doctor stalks nurse or former general criticizes modern military, etc.). It isn't really used to describe people who die. You wouldn't say my former grandmother, for example; you'd use late, as in my late grandmother. So the case of a former Titanic survivor (where someone can't really stop being a Titantic survivor in the same way they can stop being a doctor or a general) implies the rather bizarre situation of someone who survived the Titanic, but then somehow stopped surviving it. Even in dying of something else, they still survived the Titanic. So you're using former to mean "dead", rather than "stopped being suitably described by whatever follows", which isn't really right.

Another reason to drop it is that it adds nothing relevant to the headline, and headlines are meant to be concise. Consider for example: Because his previous Mercury capsule sunk Gus Grissom named his Gemini capsule after a Titanic survivor. This was the last time NASA allowed astronauts to name their capsules. It packs the same punch, but uses fewer words.
